title: Is It a Valid Search Tree?
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Return true if it is a valid binary search tree, and false otherwise.

A valid search tree follows one rule at every node: every value in its left subtree is smaller than the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is larger. The rule is about whole subtrees, not just the two children. The ordering is strict: a value equal to an ancestor's value, on either side, makes the tree invalid.

Values span the full 32-bit signed range. Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: 25 is a fine right child of 10, but it sits in the left subtree of 20, where everything must be below 20. Checking each node only against its parent misses this.
The smallest and largest 32-bit values are legal node values. Bounds that start at exactly these numbers, with a strict comparison, reject this valid tree.
The second 9 is smaller than its parent 13, but it lives in the right subtree of the root 9 and must be strictly larger than 9. Equal is not enough.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Checking each node against its two children is not enough. What does a node deep in the tree have to respect, besides its parent?
Every node lives inside an open range (low, high) set by its ancestors. Going left lowers the ceiling to the parent's value; going right raises the floor.
Recurse with check(node, low, high), starting with no bounds at all (null or ±infinity, not ±2³¹). Or do an in-order walk: the tree is valid exactly when the values come out strictly increasing.

explain.intuition:
The tempting check is local: left child smaller, right child larger. The first example shows why that fails. A node must be smaller than every ancestor it sits to the left of, and larger than every ancestor it sits to the right of. Those constraints pile up into one open interval per node. Pass the interval down: the root gets (−∞, +∞); its left child gets (−∞, root); a right grandchild of that gets (that child, root); and so on. Each node checks low < val < high, then narrows the interval for its children.

Another way to see it: an in-order walk (left, node, right) of a search tree visits values in sorted order. So the tree is valid exactly when the in-order sequence is strictly increasing, and you only need to remember the previous value. Either way, the bounds must start as "no bound", not as the smallest and largest 32-bit numbers, because those numbers are themselves legal values.
steps: Define check(node, low, high) where low and high may be missing.
If low exists and node.val ≤ low, or high exists and node.val ≥ high, return false.
Return check(node.left, low, node.val) && check(node.right, node.val, high).
pitfalls: Comparing each node only with its parent. The first example passes that test and is still invalid.
Allowing equal values with <= or a non-strict in-order check. Duplicates make the tree invalid here, as in the third example.
Starting the bounds at -2³¹ and 2³¹ - 1 with strict comparisons. A node holding exactly one of those values is then rejected; use null, ±infinity, or a 64-bit range.

solutions.title: Compare each node with its subtrees' max and min
solutions.idea: For every node, find the largest value in its left subtree and the smallest in its right subtree, and compare. Correct, but subtrees are rescanned once per ancestor.

solutions.title: Pass an open interval down
solutions.idea: Each node must lie strictly inside the range its ancestors allow. Going left lowers the upper bound, going right raises the lower bound.

solutions.title: In-order walk must be strictly increasing
solutions.idea: In-order visits a valid search tree in sorted order. Walk it with a stack and compare each value with the previous one.

followups: Exactly two values in a search tree were swapped by mistake. Find them using the in-order idea.
How would you change the check if equal values were allowed, but only in left subtrees?
